newsitem.title: USA: Ford seat decision to protect UAW relations.
newsitem.headline: Ford seat decision to protect UAW relations.

text.p: Ford Motor Co acted to protect its interests with the United Auto Workers union when it refused to accept seats made by non-union replacement workers, Ford Chief Financial Officer John Devine said Wednesday.

Devine, during a news briefing at Ford's World Headquarters, said the strike by UAW members at two Johnson Controls Inc seat assembly plants is a "problem" for the automaker because the strike has halted production of fully assembled Expedition full-size sport/utilities.
"The long-term relationship with the UAW, the long-term relationship we have with our own people is very important," Devine said.

More than 500 workers at Johnson Controls plants in Plymouth, Mich., and Oberlin, Ohio, walked off the job Tuesday morning after failing to reach agreement on a new contract. The Plymouth plant makes seats for the Expedition, made at Ford's Michigan Truck Assembly plant in Wayne, Mich. The Oberlin plant seats go into Econoline full-size vans.
Devine did not know of any contract language with Johnson Controls that would force Ford to accept seats made by replacement workers.
"We dont' think it's a legal issue," he said.
Devine added that price negotiations between Ford and Johnson over the seats are discussed separately.

Workers have been putting in temporary seats while they assemble the vehicle, then parking the Expeditions in a nearby lot. Devine said it will take about 30 minutes to put in the right seats, which will cost extra money.
Ford wants the issue settled soon so it can resume normal Expedition production. The company has not begun looking into other sources for Expedition seats, he added.
